title: Right upper quadrant pain, itch and dark urine in a 40-year-old man
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a frustrated 40-year-old man in the ED with about 10 days of a viral-type prodrome (fever, joint aches, an itchy urticarial rash and malaise), dark urine and pale stools for a week, right upper quadrant pain for 3 days and yellow eyes today. He recently shared needles. The candidate then interprets his observations, liver function and other bloods, hepatitis serology and an abdominal ultrasound report, names the diagnosis and differentials, and outlines management, public health actions, harm reduction and safety netting.
focus: Jaundice with right upper quadrant pain: taking a hepatitis risk history, reading a hepatitic LFT pattern and hepatitis B serology, and managing acute hepatitis B
diagnosis: Icteric phase of acute viral hepatitis
stem: You are an intern working in a metropolitan Emergency Department. Andrew, a 40-year-old hotel cleaner, has come in with abdominal pain. He waited a long time in the waiting room and the triage nurse says he is frustrated about it. He is now in a cubicle. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, blood results, hepatitis serology and an abdominal ultrasound report. Interpret them, give your diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Andrew, a 40-year-old hotel cleaner. You rarely go to the doctor and you are annoyed at how long you waited. You start out short and a bit irritable. If the candidate acknowledges the wait and explains what they are doing, you settle and cooperate. If they ignore it, you stay curt. You keep scratching your arms and chest. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I have this really irritating pain in my tummy and I want it fixed!"

History (give only when asked)

The pain

  • All over your tummy, but worst on the right, just under the rib cage. It does not go anywhere else.
  • It came on over about a day, 3 days ago.
  • A dull ache that comes and goes in strength.
  • 4 to 6 out of 10.
  • Nothing makes it better or worse. You have not taken any medicines for it. Leaning forward does not help. It is not worse after fatty or spicy food.
  • No injury to your tummy or chest.

Feeling unwell (give each only to a specific question)

  • The aches, the itchy welts, feeling hot, going off your food and the tiredness started about 10 days ago.
  • You feel hot, but you have not measured your temperature. No shivering attacks or shaking chills.
  • You have gone off your food because you feel awful. No weight loss.
  • All your joints ache.
  • A very itchy rash all over: "It looks like welts all over my body."
  • You are extremely tired and feel generally rotten.

Tummy and bowels

  • No pain in the upper middle of your tummy. No nausea, no vomiting, no black stools.
  • Since last week your poo has been pale, your wee has been dark like tea, and you have been itchy.
  • Only if asked about yellow skin or eyes: "I thought my eyes looked yellow this morning, but I thought I was just completely out of it."

Other systems (all negative if asked)

  • No burning or frequency when passing urine, no blood in the urine.
  • No chest pain, palpitations, cough or breathlessness.
  • No calf pain or swelling, no long trips or recent surgery.
  • No blistering rash in a band on your side.

Drugs and hepatitis risk

  • If first asked about drugs or needles: "What's that got to do with anything?" If the candidate explains why they are asking and is non-judgemental, you tell them:
  • You went to rehab for methamphetamine (ice) 10 years ago and stayed clean until 2 months ago.
  • You were laid off 2 months ago, asked a friend for some, and you shared needles with him. "Only had about 5 points, nothing since."
  • No tattoos or piercings. No sexual partners. Never had a blood transfusion.
  • No travel overseas, including Africa or South America. Nobody around you has been unwell or yellow, and you know of no food scares.

Past history

  • Rehab 10 years ago, as above. Nothing else.
  • No known gallstones. You have not taken any paracetamol, and you have never taken an overdose. No anti-inflammatories. No recent drinking binges.

Medications: none. No herbal or bodybuilding supplements.

Allergies: none.

Family history: "Not sure. I moved out when I was a teenager."

Social history

  • You work as a cleaner in a hotel, a new job since being laid off. You live alone.
  • You smoke 5 cigarettes a day and have since your teens.
  • You drink 1 to 2 bottles of wine a week, sometimes a cask, but less since the new job.
  • Injecting as above.

Ideas, concerns, expectations

  • Ideas: "I feel like something's definitely not right." If pressed for what you think it is: "You tell me, doc, that's why I'm here."
  • Concerns: "This whole thing has thrown me out of sorts. It's making it hard to stay on track." If the candidate gently asks what staying on track means: "Staying off the gear. Losing my job nearly sent me straight back."
  • Expectations: "I'm hoping you can tell me what's wrong so I can get on with it."

Questions to raise in Part 1: "How much longer is this going to take?" and, if the candidate asks about needles, "Am I in trouble for telling you that?"

The nurse and how Andrew changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the ones under Exam findings.
  • Partway through, the nurse says: "He's been asking at the desk how much longer he'll be. He says he might just go home."
  • If the candidate offers analgesia or something for the itch, Andrew says "Finally" and becomes more cooperative; a few minutes later his pain is about 3 out of 10.
  • If the candidate asks for bloods, serology or imaging in Part 1, the examiner says the results will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (examiner gives each only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • Observations (triage set at 10:40, given by the nurse): HR 96 regular, BP 132/80, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.8 °C, BGL 5.6 mmol/L.
  • General: tired, irritable, scratching. Visibly jaundiced. Alert and fully oriented.
  • Skin: raised, red, blanching wheals (urticaria) over the trunk and limbs with scratch marks. No spider naevi, no bruising or petechiae.
  • Eyes: yellow sclerae.
  • Hands: no clubbing, palmar erythema, leuconychia or Dupuytren's contracture. No asterixis.
  • Arms: a few healing puncture marks in the left antecubital fossa. No abscess, cellulitis or thrombophlebitis.
  • Chest wall: no gynaecomastia. No loss of body hair.
  • Joints: aches on movement of the knees and wrists, but no swelling, warmth or effusion.
  • Lymph nodes: no lymphadenopathy.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended. No caput medusae, scars or visible veins.
  • Palpation: tender in the right upper quadrant. Liver edge smooth, soft and tender, 3 cm below the right costal margin. Murphy's sign negative. No guarding or rebound. Spleen not palpable. Kidneys not ballotable.
  • Percussion: liver span 15 cm. No shifting dullness.
  • Auscultation: normal bowel sounds.
  • PR (if requested): pale, clay-coloured stool on the glove. No blood or melaena.
  • Heart and lungs: normal. Chest clear at both bases.
  • Urine dipstick (if requested): dark urine; bilirubin 2+; no blood, leucocytes or nitrites.
  • ECG (if requested): sinus rhythm 96/min, normal axis and intervals, no ST or T wave changes.
  • Everything else normal.

check.x: Professionalism

Washes hands, introduces self and confirms identity. Acknowledges Andrew's frustration about the wait calmly, without becoming defensive, explains what will happen next and offers analgesia or something for the itch early.
Asks about drug use and needle sharing in a non-judgemental way: explains why the question matters for his symptoms, reassures him about confidentiality and that he is not in trouble.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site: generalised, worst in the right upper quadrant under the ribs, no radiation
Onset, character and severity: came on over about a day, 3 days ago; dull fluctuating ache; 4 to 6 out of 10
Modifying factors: nothing helps or worsens it, no medication tried, not eased by leaning forward, not worse with fatty or spicy food

check.x: Elicits the prodromal symptoms, starting about 10 days ago, at least 4 of: feeling hot, reduced appetite, aches in all joints, a very itchy urticarial (welt-like) rash, extreme fatigue and malaise; and checks for weight loss.
Asks specifically about cholestasis and jaundice and elicits pale stools, dark tea-coloured urine and itch since last week, and yellow eyes this morning.

Screens the GI tract (epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, melaena) and asks questions to exclude differentials from at least 3 other systems: urinary (pyelonephritis), cardiac (inferior MI), respiratory (basal pneumonia, PE risk), trauma, shingles.
Takes a viral hepatitis risk history:
check.d: Critical: the injecting and needle-sharing history must be elicited.

kids.x: Injecting drug use: methamphetamine 2 months ago with shared needles, about 5 points, nothing since
Travel to endemic areas or other hepatitis A exposures (contaminated food, unwell contacts)

check.x: Asks about hepatotoxins and biliary causes: paracetamol use or overdose, NSAIDs, other medicines or supplements, recent alcohol binges and known gallstones.
check.d: Critical: must ask about paracetamol use or overdose and alcohol; plus at least 2 of NSAIDs, other medicines or supplements, known gallstones.

check.x: Takes a past medical, medication and allergy history: rehab for methamphetamine 10 years ago, clean until 2 months ago; no medications; no allergies.
Takes a social history including alcohol quantity, smoking, work and living situation; family history.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations, including what "hard to stay on track" means (his fear of relapse) and his wish to know what is wrong.
Examination
General inspection and skin: identifies jaundice (yellow sclerae) and the urticarial wheals with scratch marks.
check.d: Critical: must identify jaundice (scleral icterus); the urticaria and scratch marks are expected but not critical.

check.x: Asks for the vital signs: low-grade temperature 37.8 °C, HR 96, BP 132/80 (triage set; repeat at 11:45 similar).
Looks for stigmata of chronic liver disease (clubbing, palmar erythema, leuconychia, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, caput medusae) and inspects the arms for injection sites and their complications.
Assesses for hepatic encephalopathy: checks orientation and conscious state and tests for asterixis.
Palpates the abdomen and the liver: right upper quadrant tenderness, a smooth tender liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin, and tests Murphy's sign (negative); no guarding or rebound.
Completes the examination: spleen, liver span by percussion, shifting dullness, chest; requests urine dipstick and ECG.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: all values in the white zone at both times with a low-grade temperature, so no chart escalation is triggered, and plans repeat observations, BGL and conscious state.
Interprets the LFTs as a hepatitic (hepatocellular) pattern: bilirubin 185 with ALT 1635 and AST 1610 (more than 40 times the upper limit) and ALP and GGT only mildly raised.
States that synthetic function is preserved (INR 1.0; albumin normal), so there is no acute liver failure now.

Interprets the other results: paracetamol undetectable, normal lipase, normal WCC with only a mild CRP rise; hepatitis A IgM negative; a negative HCV antibody does not exclude recent hepatitis C because of the window period, so HCV RNA is needed.
Interprets the hepatitis B serology:
check.d: Critical: HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc must be interpreted correctly.

kids.x: HBsAg positive: current hepatitis B infection
HBeAg positive: active viral replication, highly infectious
Anti-HBs negative: not immune and not yet resolved

check.x: Interprets the ultrasound: no gallstones, no intra- or extrahepatic duct dilatation and patent hepatic vessels on Doppler, so no biliary obstruction, making cholangitis and Budd-Chiari unlikely; mild hepatomegaly with reactive gallbladder wall thickening.

Gives the diagnosis as acute hepatitis B in the icteric phase, most likely acquired from shared needles 2 months ago, justified by the prodrome (fever, arthralgia, urticaria, malaise), jaundice with dark urine and pale stools, tender hepatomegaly, the hepatitic LFTs and the serology.

Gives at least 2 differentials with a feature for or against each, including ascending cholangitis (Charcot's triad, but no rigors, normal WCC, hepatocellular pattern and no duct dilatation), and others such as acute hepatitis C, hepatitis A, paracetamol or drug-induced liver injury, or alcohol-related hepatitis.
Management

Plans supportive care: oral fluids and diet as tolerated, analgesia that avoids hepatotoxins and sedatives (no NSAIDs, paracetamol only at a reduced dose agreed with the senior team), a non-sedating antihistamine for itch, and no alcohol.

Monitors for acute liver failure: repeat INR, bilirubin, LFTs and glucose, and checks conscious state for encephalopathy; escalates for a rising INR, confusion, hypoglycaemia or vomiting with inability to keep fluids down.

Discusses with the gastroenterology or hepatology team for specialist follow-up, and decides disposition: early outpatient review is possible with a normal INR, no encephalopathy, adequate oral intake and reliable follow-up; otherwise admits.

Completes the blood-borne virus screen: HIV with his consent, HCV RNA, and hepatitis A immunity (offers vaccination if not immune). Hepatitis D antibody (HBsAg positive and injects drugs) is an optional extra, not required for the mark.

Recognises hepatitis B as notifiable (the laboratory notifies; the clinician notifies or contacts the public health unit as local law requires) and liaises with the public health unit about contact tracing, including testing of the friend he shared needles with (likely source).
check.d: Critical: recognises hepatitis B is notifiable and involves the public health unit, and arranges testing of the friend he shared needles with. Vaccination of non-immune contacts, and HBIG within 72 hours (percutaneous) or 14 days (sexual), is credit-worthy but not required.

check.x: Offers harm reduction and support without judgement: needle and syringe program, referral to drug and alcohol services, and acknowledges his concern about relapse.
Explanation, safety netting and follow-up
Explains the diagnosis to Andrew in plain words: a virus infecting the liver, probably from the shared needles; most adults clear it on their own; blood tests will check that the liver is coping.
Gives red flags and how to avoid passing it on, in plain words:

kids.x: At least 4 red flags: confusion, drowsiness or behaviour change; bleeding or easy bruising; vomiting and unable to keep fluids down; worsening jaundice or pain; high fever or shakes; and to return to ED straight away or call 000 if they occur
While infectious: no sharing of needles or other injecting equipment, razors or toothbrushes; condoms with any partner; cover cuts; no blood donation

check.x: Arranges follow-up: repeat LFTs and INR within a few days, hepatology clinic review and GP follow-up, and repeat HBsAg at 6 months to confirm clearance (persisting HBsAg at 6 months means chronic hepatitis B).

part2.lead: Here are Andrew's observations, his blood results, his hepatitis serology and the abdominal ultrasound report.
part2.patient:
Andrew speaks only during the fourth question, when the candidate explains what happens before he goes home. He asks:

  • "Do you have to tell anyone? Will my boss find out?"
  • "Can I still have a drink?"

If the candidate is non-judgemental he relaxes and agrees to see drug and alcohol services and to visit the needle and syringe program. If the candidate lectures him, he becomes defensive: "I knew I shouldn't have said anything." If the candidate uses jargon such as "surface antigen" or "notifiable", ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air throughout. Tolerating oral fluids.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: the 11:45 pain score is blank on the chart. If analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate it is 3 and analgesia has been given; otherwise it is 5 and none has been given.
  • Read: at 10:40 RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 132/80, HR 96, temperature 37.8 °C and alert: all in the white zone. At 11:45 similar (HR 92, temperature 37.6 °C). BGL 5.6.
  • Meaning: haemodynamically stable with a low-grade fever, which fits the viral prodrome. No chart value calls for a clinical review or rapid response. A white zone chart does not exclude cholangitis or evolving liver failure, so it must be read with the bloods.
  • Changes: continue regular observations with conscious state and BGL (hypoglycaemia and confusion are signs of liver failure); clinical review for any yellow zone value, rapid response for red, and senior review for new confusion.

rows.note: Triage: abdominal pain and yellow eyes. Triage bloods taken.
Repeat set. Waiting over an hour, frustrated, scratching, asking how much longer. Pain score: see examiner.

handover.label: Liver function, coagulation and other bloods
handover.result: Collected 10:40. Haemolysis index normal. ALT and AST phoned to ED at 11:40.
handover.model:
• Read: bilirubin 185 (about 10 times normal) with ALT 1635 and AST 1610 (more than 40 times the upper limit), while ALP 220 and GGT 75 are only mildly raised: the transaminase rise far outweighs the ALP rise, a hepatocellular (hepatitic) pattern. INR 1.0 and albumin 38 are normal. FBC normal with no leucocytosis; CRP 12 mildly raised. Lipase, renal function, electrolytes, calcium, phosphate, magnesium and glucose normal. Paracetamol not detected.
  • Meaning: acute hepatocellular injury with jaundice; transaminases above 1000 point to viral hepatitis, drug or toxin injury (paracetamol) or ischaemia, not alcohol alone, and only rarely to biliary obstruction: a passing common bile duct stone can briefly do this, which is why the ultrasound is still needed. Synthetic function is preserved (normal INR), so there is no acute liver failure now. A normal WCC argues against cholangitis; a normal lipase against pancreatitis.
  • Changes: repeat INR, LFTs and glucose to follow the trend; avoid hepatotoxins and alcohol; a rising INR or encephalopathy would mean admission and urgent hepatology input.

handover.label: Hepatitis serology
handover.result: Added on to the 10:40 sample by the ED team; urgent request, results 13:15. HBsAg reactive, confirmed on a second assay. HCV antibody may not yet be detectable after a recent exposure; HCV RNA testing is suggested if clinically indicated.
handover.model:
• Read: HBsAg detected; total anti-HBc and IgM anti-HBc detected; HBeAg detected, anti-HBe not detected; anti-HBs not detected. Hepatitis A IgM not detected. HCV antibody not detected.
  • Meaning: HBsAg means current hepatitis B infection; IgM anti-HBc means it is acute (recent); HBeAg means active viral replication and high infectivity; no anti-HBs means he is neither immune nor yet recovered. This is acute hepatitis B, which fits needle sharing 2 months ago (incubation 1 to 6 months). Hepatitis A is excluded as the cause. A negative HCV antibody does not exclude hepatitis C acquired 2 months ago (window period).
  • Changes: hepatitis B is notifiable (the laboratory notifies; the clinician notifies or contacts the public health unit as local law requires); liaise with the public health unit about contact tracing: test the friend he shared needles with (likely source), and test and vaccinate any recent sexual, household or needle-sharing contacts, with HBIG if non-immune and exposed within 72 hours (percutaneous) or 14 days (sexual); send HCV RNA and HIV (with consent), and optionally hepatitis D antibody; infection-control advice; repeat HBsAg at 6 months to confirm clearance.

handover.label: Abdominal ultrasound
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the upper abdomen with Doppler of the hepatic vessels. 12:30.

Clinical details: 40-year-old man. 3 days of right upper quadrant pain, low-grade fever, jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. Bilirubin 185, ALT 1635. Murphy's sign negative. ?Biliary obstruction ?Cholangitis.

Findings:

  • Liver: mildly enlarged at 17 cm in the midclavicular line, with a smooth outline. Diffusely reduced parenchymal echogenicity with accentuated brightness of the portal venule walls. No focal lesion. No surface nodularity.
  • Gallbladder: contracted, with a diffusely thickened, oedematous wall of 6 mm. No gallstones or sludge. No pericholecystic fluid. Sonographic Murphy's sign negative.
  • Bile ducts: common bile duct 4 mm. No intrahepatic duct dilatation. No choledocholithiasis seen.
  • Doppler: portal vein patent with normal forward (hepatopetal) flow. Hepatic veins patent with normal phasic flow. Hepatic artery patent.
  • Spleen: normal size, 11.5 cm.
  • Pancreas: visualised head and body normal.
  • Kidneys: normal size and appearance. No hydronephrosis.
  • Peritoneum: no ascites.

Conclusion: mild hepatomegaly with diffuse parenchymal change and gallbladder wall thickening without gallstones, a non-specific appearance that can be seen with acute hepatocellular inflammation. No biliary dilatation or gallstones. Hepatic and portal veins patent. No splenomegaly or ascites.
handover.model:
• Read: smooth, mildly enlarged liver with diffusely reduced echogenicity and no focal lesion or nodularity; contracted, thick-walled gallbladder with no stones, sludge or pericholecystic fluid and a negative sonographic Murphy's; CBD 4 mm, no duct dilatation; portal and hepatic veins patent; no splenomegaly or ascites.
  • Meaning: no biliary obstruction, so jaundice is hepatocellular, not obstructive; cholangitis and choledocholithiasis are very unlikely despite Charcot's triad. Gallbladder wall thickening without stones is a recognised reactive finding in acute hepatitis, not cholecystitis. Patent hepatic veins exclude Budd-Chiari. No nodularity, splenomegaly or ascites argues against chronic liver disease.
  • Changes: no ERCP, surgical referral or antibiotics needed; supports managing this as acute viral hepatitis.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Andrew, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Andrew now, here in the emergency department.
Before Andrew goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Andrew, 40.
  • Situation: acute icteric hepatitis; serology shows acute hepatitis B, HBeAg positive; synthetic function preserved; requesting review and follow-up.
  • Background: prodrome of fever, arthralgia, urticaria and malaise for about 10 days; a week of dark urine, pale stools and itch; 3 days of RUQ ache; yellow eyes today. Shared needles injecting methamphetamine 2 months ago. 1 to 2 bottles of wine a week; no medicines, no paracetamol. Jaundiced, tender smooth liver 3 cm, Murphy's negative, no asterixis or stigmata.
  • Assessment: obs stable, T 37.8; hepatocellular LFTs (ALT 1635, bili 185) with INR 1.0; paracetamol nil, WCC normal; acute HBV serology (HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, HBeAg +, anti-HBs −); HAV IgM negative; HCV Ab negative but within the window period, so HCV RNA is needed; US no obstruction, vessels patent.
  • Recommendation: advice on admission versus early clinic review; repeat INR; I will contact the public health unit about contact tracing.

Acute hepatitis B (icteric phase): needle sharing 2 months ago; prodrome of fever, arthralgia, urticaria and malaise; jaundice, dark urine, pale stools; tender smooth hepatomegaly; transaminases above 1000; HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc positive.

  • Ascending cholangitis (must not miss): for: fever, RUQ pain, jaundice (Charcot's triad); against: no rigors, haemodynamically stable, normal WCC with only a mild CRP rise, transaminases far above the ALP, viral prodrome, no duct dilatation or stones on ultrasound.
  • Paracetamol or drug-induced liver injury (must not miss): against: denies use, level undetectable.
  • Acute hepatitis C: for: shared needles; antibody negative but window period, needs HCV RNA.
  • Hepatitis A: against: IgM negative (no travel is weaker; it also spreads among people who inject drugs).
  • Alcohol-related hepatitis: for: wine and casks; against: transaminases above 1000, AST:ALT about 1.

1. Supportive care: oral fluids and diet as tolerated; analgesia avoiding NSAIDs and sedatives (paracetamol only at a reduced dose agreed with seniors); non-sedating antihistamine for itch; no alcohol.
  2. Monitor for liver failure: repeat INR, bilirubin, LFTs and glucose; conscious state and asterixis; escalate a rising INR, confusion, hypoglycaemia or vomiting.
  3. Gastroenterology or hepatology discussion and disposition: with normal INR, no encephalopathy, oral intake and reliable follow-up, early outpatient review; otherwise admit.
  4. Notifiable: the laboratory notifies; contact the public health unit about contact tracing (test the friend he shared needles with). Send HCV RNA, HIV (with consent) and hepatitis A immunity; hepatitis D antibody is an optional extra (HBsAg positive and injects drugs).

• Plain explanation: a virus infecting the liver, probably from the shared needles; most adults clear it over weeks to months.
  • Come back to ED straight away or call 000: confusion or drowsiness, bleeding or bruising, vomiting and unable to keep fluids down, worsening yellowing or pain.
  • Avoid passing it on: no sharing needles, injecting equipment, razors or toothbrushes; condoms; cover cuts; no blood donation.
  • Contacts: notification is confidential and his employer is not told; his friend is offered testing.
  • "Can I still have a drink?": no alcohol while the liver recovers.
  • Follow-up: LFTs and INR in a few days; hepatology and GP; HBsAg at 6 months.
  • Support: needle and syringe program, drug and alcohol referral.

ddx.for: He shared needles 2 months ago, had a prodrome of fever, arthralgia, urticaria and malaise, now has jaundice with dark urine and pale stools and a tender smooth liver, with ALT 1635 and HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc and HBeAg positive.
He has fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice, which is Charcot's triad.
ddx.against: No rigors, haemodynamically stable, normal WCC with only a mild CRP rise, transaminase rise far greater than the ALP rise, a viral prodrome, and no duct dilatation or stones on ultrasound.

ddx.dx: Paracetamol or other drug-induced liver injury
ddx.for: Transaminases above 1000 can come from paracetamol toxicity.
ddx.against: He denies any paracetamol, overdose, other medicines or supplements, and the paracetamol level is undetectable.
The HCV antibody is negative, although this can be falsely reassuring in the window period, and the hepatitis B serology already explains the illness.

ddx.for: He has a hepatitic picture with jaundice after a febrile prodrome.
ddx.against: Hepatitis A IgM is negative (no travel is a weaker point; hepatitis A also spreads among people who inject drugs).

ddx.for: He drinks 1 to 2 bottles of wine a week and sometimes a cask.
ddx.against: He reports no recent binges, his transaminases are above 1000 with an AST:ALT ratio of about 1, and the GGT is only mildly raised.

guide:
In Part 1, Andrew starts out frustrated and settles only if the candidate acknowledges the wait. He gives the drug and needle history only if asked directly and without judgement. If first asked about drugs, he says "What's that got to do with anything?" and discloses once the candidate explains why it matters. He gives the jaundice comment only if asked about yellow skin or eyes. Partway through, the nurse reports that he is talking about leaving. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. If the candidate asks for bloods, serology or imaging, say the results will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the observations, the bloods, the serology and the ultrasound report, then ask all four questions in order. The 11:45 pain score is blank: give 3 if analgesia was ordered in Part 1, otherwise 5. Andrew puts his two questions only during the fourth question, while the candidate explains what happens before he goes home.

A high-performing candidate defuses the frustration, characterises the pain, and draws out the prodrome (fever, arthralgia, urticaria, malaise) and the cholestatic symptoms. They take a full hepatitis risk history, elicit the needle sharing sensitively, and ask about paracetamol and alcohol. They examine for jaundice, stigmata of chronic liver disease, injection sites, asterixis, liver size and Murphy's sign. In Part 2 they read the hepatitic LFT pattern with preserved synthetic function, interpret each hepatitis B marker correctly, use the ultrasound to exclude obstruction and cholangitis, and name acute hepatitis B. Their management is supportive with monitoring for liver failure, and they cover notification, contact tracing, the HIV and HCV RNA screen, harm reduction and a 6-month HBsAg check.

A borderline candidate takes the pain history but misses the needle sharing or asks about it judgementally. They do not check for asterixis or Murphy's sign. They may misread HBeAg or anti-HBs, call this cholecystitis, or start antibiotics and ask for an ERCP. They may forget notification, contacts, harm reduction or the 6-month follow-up.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute hepatitis B, icteric phase

Andrew shared needles 2 months ago, which fits the 1 to 6 month incubation of hepatitis B. About 10 days ago he then had a classic viral hepatitis prodrome: anorexia, malaise and fever, with urticaria and arthralgia, followed by right upper quadrant pain. Urticaria and arthralgia are particularly typical of hepatitis B and are thought to be immune complex mediated. He has now entered the icteric phase: dark urine, then pale stools and itch, then visible jaundice, with a tender smooth enlarged liver. His LFTs show hepatocellular injury, and the serology confirms acute hepatitis B.

The stages of acute viral hepatitis

  • Incubation: 1 to 6 months for hepatitis B.
  • Prodrome: anorexia, malaise, nausea, distaste for cigarettes, fever and RUQ pain; urticaria and arthralgia especially in hepatitis B.
  • Icteric phase: dark urine, then jaundice 3 to 10 days later, often as the other symptoms ease. Tender smooth hepatomegaly; mild splenomegaly in 15 to 20%. Jaundice peaks at 1 to 2 weeks.
  • Recovery: symptoms settle over weeks; biochemical recovery from hepatitis B usually takes 1 to 4 months, and HBsAg is normally cleared within 6 months (anti-HBs then appears).

History and examination

Abdominal pain needs a screen of causes outside the abdomen: inferior MI (Andrew smokes), lower lobe pneumonia or PE, pyelonephritis, trauma and shingles. The hepatitis risk history covers injecting and needle sharing, tattoos and piercings, sexual partners, blood products, and travel and other hepatitis A exposures. Hepatitis A spreads by the faecal-oral route: it is endemic in many low-income countries, and in Australia outbreaks also occur among people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, and through contaminated food. Always ask about paracetamol, overdose, NSAIDs, supplements, alcohol and gallstones. Ask about drug use without judgement and explain why it matters; patients disclose more when they do not feel judged. On examination, look for jaundice, stigmata of chronic liver disease, injection sites and their complications, and asterixis or confusion (encephalopathy). Assess liver size and Murphy's sign.

Andrew meets Charcot's triad

Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice make up Charcot's triad, so ascending cholangitis must be actively excluded. Against cholangitis: he has no rigors and is haemodynamically stable, the WCC is normal with only a mild CRP rise, the transaminase rise is far greater than the ALP rise, he had a viral prodrome, and the ultrasound shows no duct dilatation or stones. Murphy's sign is not a test for cholangitis (it is often negative in cholangitis); it tests for gallbladder inflammation, and his negative Murphy's sign, with no stones or pericholecystic fluid, argues against acute cholecystitis. A thickened gallbladder wall without stones is a recognised reactive finding in acute hepatitis and is not cholecystitis.

Interpreting the LFTs

Transaminases more than 40 times the upper limit with only a mild rise in ALP and GGT is a hepatitic (hepatocellular) pattern. Transaminases above 1000 suggest viral hepatitis, drug or toxin injury (especially paracetamol) or ischaemic hepatitis. Alcohol alone rarely causes them. A passing common bile duct stone can briefly do this, which is why the ultrasound is still needed. Bilirubin and transaminases reflect injury, not function. The INR (with glucose and conscious state) reflects acute synthetic function; albumin falls only slowly and mostly reflects chronic disease or nutrition. Here the INR is normal, the glucose is normal and he is alert, so there is no acute liver failure. Acute liver failure means coagulopathy (INR 1.5 or more) with encephalopathy, so INR, glucose and conscious state are the values to follow.

Interpreting hepatitis B serology

MarkerAndrewMeaning
HBsAgPositiveCurrent infection (acute or chronic)
Anti-HBc totalPositivePast or current infection (never from vaccination)
IgM anti-HBcPositiveAcute (recent) infection
HBeAgPositiveActive replication, highly infectious
Anti-HBsNegativeNot immune and not resolved; appears after clearance or vaccination

A vaccinated person is anti-HBs positive with negative HBsAg and anti-HBc. A person who has cleared past infection is anti-HBc and anti-HBs positive with negative HBsAg. Chronic hepatitis B is HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months. A negative HCV antibody 2 months after exposure does not exclude hepatitis C, so HCV RNA is sent. HIV testing is done with consent.

Differentials

  • Ascending cholangitis: excluded as above.
  • Paracetamol or drug-induced liver injury: always check a paracetamol level when transaminases are very high. His is undetectable.
  • Acute hepatitis C: same exposure. Often asymptomatic. Needs HCV RNA in the window period.
  • Hepatitis A: the negative IgM excludes it; no travel is a weaker point, because hepatitis A also spreads among people who inject drugs.
  • Alcohol-related hepatitis: transaminases are usually below 300 to 400, with AST higher than ALT.

Management

Acute hepatitis B in adults is managed supportively, and most adults clear it. Treatment:

  • Fluids and nutrition as tolerated.
  • Avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs, and avoid sedatives that can mask encephalopathy.
  • A non-sedating antihistamine for itch.

Monitor INR, bilirubin and conscious state for liver failure, and refer to a hepatitis or gastroenterology service. Antiviral treatment is reserved for severe acute hepatitis B (for example coagulopathy or features of liver failure) under specialist care. Admit if the INR is rising, there is any encephalopathy, he cannot keep up oral intake, or safe follow-up cannot be arranged.

Public health: hepatitis B is notifiable in every Australian state and territory. The friend he shared needles with is the likely source and is offered testing. Any recent sexual, household or needle-sharing contacts are offered testing and hepatitis B vaccination and, if non-immune, hepatitis B immunoglobulin, ideally within 72 hours of a percutaneous exposure and within 14 days of a sexual exposure, as set out in the Australian Immunisation Handbook. Notification is confidential.

Harm reduction: needle and syringe programs, referral to drug and alcohol services, and screening for HCV and HIV. Offer hepatitis A vaccination if he is not immune, as recommended for people who inject drugs. As an optional extra, hepatitis D antibody can be tested: ASHM advises testing HBsAg-positive people with risk factors such as injecting drug use, because co-infection worsens acute hepatitis.

Safety netting and follow-up

Andrew should return to ED, or call 000, for confusion or drowsiness, bleeding or bruising, persistent vomiting, worsening jaundice or pain, or high fever. While he is HBsAg and HBeAg positive he is highly infectious:

  • No sharing of injecting equipment, razors or toothbrushes.
  • Condoms with any partner.
  • Cover cuts.
  • No blood donation.

Repeat LFTs and INR within a few days. Follow up in the hepatology clinic and with his GP, with HBsAg rechecked at 6 months to confirm clearance. HBsAg that persists beyond 6 months means chronic hepatitis B and long-term specialist follow-up.
points: Viral hepatitis has a prodrome (anorexia, malaise, fever, RUQ pain; urticaria and arthralgia especially in hepatitis B), then an icteric phase with dark urine, pale stools, itch and jaundice.

Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice make up Charcot's triad: always exclude cholangitis with the WCC/CRP, the LFT pattern and an ultrasound looking for duct dilatation and stones; a negative Murphy's sign argues against acute cholecystitis.
Transaminases above 1000 with a relatively small ALP rise is a hepatitic pattern. Think viral hepatitis, paracetamol or other drug injury, or ischaemia, and always check a paracetamol level.
Bilirubin and transaminases measure injury; INR, glucose and conscious state measure acute liver function (albumin falls only slowly). A normal INR and no encephalopathy means no acute liver failure.
HBsAg means current infection, IgM anti-HBc means acute infection, HBeAg means high infectivity, and anti-HBs means immunity or recovery. HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months means chronic hepatitis B.

Acute hepatitis B is notifiable. Management is supportive monitoring, contact tracing with testing and vaccination (and HBIG within the time window for non-immune contacts), HCV RNA and HIV testing, harm reduction, and repeat HBsAg at 6 months.
